title: Testing, validation & logbooks
blurb: Daily, weekly, quarterly and annual tests on sterilizers, washer-disinfectors and ultrasonics, and the records that prove it.
question: It's 8 am and you are first in. Before the first patient's instruments go into the vacuum (type B) sterilizer, which tests must you carry out and record, and what do you do if one fails?

teach.body: Validation proves that a machine can achieve the right conditions (temperature, pressure and time) for its loads. It is done at installation and then yearly by a Competent Person (Decontamination) or service engineer. Routine periodic tests prove it still does, day after day. The daily and weekly tests are done by the user or, by delegation, the operator: often the dental nurse. If a machine fails any test it is withdrawn from service, advice is sought, and instruments from a failed cycle are not used.

Test
Types
Who
teach.caption: Each level includes the tests below it: weekly includes the daily tests, quarterly includes the weekly ones, and so on. Follow the manufacturer's schedule if it differs.

teach.body: Automatic control test (every type): run a cycle and check 'cycle complete' shows, the temperature, pressure and hold time stayed within the limits set at validation, then record them with the date and your signature. Steam penetration test (vacuum types B and S only): a Helix or Bowie-Dick test proves the vacuum removes enough air for steam to reach hollow and wrapped loads. In a Helix test the indicator strip sits at the end of a long, narrow tube: an even colour change passes; a patchy one fails.

items.label: Sterilizer: automatic control test, plus steam penetration (B, S). Washer-disinfector and ultrasonic: clean strainers, check cleaning visually.
Sterilizer: air leakage (B, S) or residual air (S, N). Washer-disinfector and ultrasonic: protein residue test, door-seal checks.
By CP(D) or engineer: thermometric tests; ultrasonic activity (foil) test.
Full revalidation of every machine by CP(D) or engineer.

teach.h: Chemical indicators show exposure, not sterility
teach.body: The indicator printed on a pouch or on tape changes colour when it has been exposed to the process. That tells you the pack went through a cycle. It does not prove the contents are sterile. If an indicator hasn't changed, don't use the pack: set it aside and investigate. A load is released only when the indicator has changed, the cycle record shows every parameter was met, and the pack is dry and intact.

teach.caption: A gap at any step (missing print-out, unchanged indicator, damp pack) means the load or pack is held back and investigated.

Nine foil strips hang in a 3 × 3 grid, each no more than 10 mm above the tank floor. A pass shows similar erosion on all nine. Here the front-right strip is untouched, so part of the tank isn't cleaning: withdraw the machine for repair.

items: Fill the tank to the right level, add any detergent the manufacturer specifies, and bring it to operating temperature.
Tape nine foil strips across the top in a 3 × 3 grid, each ending no more than 10 mm above, but not touching, the floor.
Run for the set exposure time (typically 30 seconds to 10 minutes, depending on the machine).
Remove, blot dry and compare the strips. Keep them as a record.
Drain and clean the tank to remove the foil debris.

teach.h: If it isn't written down, it didn't happen
teach.body: Each sterilizer has a logbook covering its whole life: maintenance, validation, faults, modifications and routine tests. Every cycle is recorded, by print-out, data logger or, if there's no printer, by hand: date, cycle completed without a failure light, temperature and pressure achieved, and operator's signature. Print-outs fade, so copy them. Keep records for at least two years. If a print-out is missing, quarantine that load and report it. Decontamination is audited at least every six months.

teach.text: The steam penetration (Helix or Bowie-Dick) test is only for vacuum sterilizers, types B and S. A type N has no vacuum stage, so its daily test is the automatic control test alone. Every type needs the automatic control test.

items: Validation (at installation, then yearly) proves the machine works; routine tests prove it still does.
Daily: automatic control test (all types) plus steam penetration (B and S only).
Weekly: air leakage (B, S) and residual air (S, N); protein residue test on washers and ultrasonics.
Foil test: nine strips in a 3 × 3 grid; even erosion passes, no erosion means withdraw it.
Chemical indicator = exposed to the process, not proof of sterility. Record every cycle; keep records 2 years.

summary: You can now tell validation from routine testing, list the daily, weekly, quarterly and annual tests for sterilizers, washer-disinfectors and ultrasonic cleaners, carry out and interpret the automatic control, steam penetration and foil ablation tests, and keep the records that prove it was all done.

A.q: Which daily test confirms that a benchtop sterilizer reached its correct temperature, pressure and hold time?
A.why: The automatic control test, done daily on all benchtop types, checks the cycle values stay within the limits set at validation.

whyNot.0: The protein residue test checks cleaning in washer-disinfectors and ultrasonics, weekly.
whyNot.1: Air leakage is a weekly test for vacuum sterilizers.
whyNot.2: The foil test checks ultrasonic cleaner activity.

A.q: The indicator on a pouch has changed to the expected colour. What does this tell you?
options: The pack was exposed to the process
The pouch can be stored for two years
A.why: An external chemical indicator shows the pack has been through the process conditions, not that the contents are sterile.

whyNot.0: Indicators show exposure only; release also depends on the cycle record and pack integrity.
whyNot.2: Wrapped storage is up to one year, and the indicator says nothing about storage.
whyNot.3: Validation is a separate engineering process recorded in the logbook.

A.q: During a foil ablation test, one of the nine foil strips shows no erosion at all. What should happen?
options: Withdraw the ultrasonic cleaner from use
Repeat the test with a longer cycle
Move instruments away from that corner of the tank
Add more detergent and carry on
A.why: HTM 01-05 says no erosion indicates failure (likely a transducer). Withdraw the cleaner and send it for repair or replace it.

whyNot.1: Lengthening the test hides a fault rather than fixing it.
whyNot.2: Avoiding part of the tank is not a safe workaround for a failed machine.
whyNot.3: Detergent doesn't fix a failed transducer.

B.q: Which sterilizer does NOT need a daily steam penetration (Helix or Bowie-Dick) test?
B.why: Steam penetration tests are for vacuum sterilizers only (B and S). A type N has no vacuum stage.

whyNot.0: Type B sterilizers need a daily steam penetration test.
whyNot.1: Type S sterilizers also need it daily.
whyNot.3: Pouches go in vacuum sterilizers, which do need the test.

B.q: The print-out for this morning's sterilizer load is missing. What is the best action?
options: Release the load, as the display said complete
Quarantine the load and report it
Write the usual values in the logbook
Use the load only for routine check-ups
B.why: Without a cycle record you can't prove the parameters were met, so the load is quarantined and the problem reported.

whyNot.0: Release depends on evidence that every parameter was met.
whyNot.2: Writing in values you didn't see is falsifying a record.
whyNot.3: Every patient needs properly processed instruments.

B.q: How often should a washer-disinfector have a protein residue test?
B.why: The protein residue test is a weekly user test on washer-disinfectors (and ultrasonic cleaners).

whyNot.0: Daily checks are cleaning the strainers and a visual check of cleaning.
whyNot.2: Two years is far too long between tests.
whyNot.3: Testing continues throughout the machine's life, not just at installation.

C.q: A pouch indicator has NOT changed colour after the cycle. What should this be taken to mean?
options: The pack must be investigated, not used
The pack is sterile but the ink is faulty
The pack can be used on low-risk patients
The pack only needs a new label
C.why: No change means you have no evidence the pack was exposed to the process. Don't use it; investigate and reprocess.

whyNot.1: You can't assume sterility when the indicator hasn't changed.
whyNot.2: There is no 'low-risk' exemption from correctly processed instruments.
whyNot.3: Re-labelling doesn't address the possible process failure.

C.q: The sterilizer has no automatic printer. Which of these must you record by hand for each cycle?
options: The patient's name and date of birth
C.why: HTM 01-05 lists date, satisfactory completion of the cycle, temperature/pressure achieved and the operator's signature.

whyNot.0: Patient details don't go in the sterilizer process log.
whyNot.1: Detergent batches aren't part of the sterilizer cycle record.
whyNot.2: Room conditions aren't required in the cycle record.

C.q: Who normally carries out the quarterly thermometric tests on a sterilizer?
C.why: Quarterly and annual tests are performed by a Competent Person (Decontamination) or service engineer.

whyNot.1: Nurses do the daily and weekly user tests, not thermometric testing.
whyNot.3: Waste contractors deal with waste, not equipment testing.

reteach.title: Think of an MOT and your daily car checks
reteach.question: You check your car's lights and tyres yourself, but a garage does the MOT. How does that match sterilizer testing?

blocks.body: Before a long drive you check the lights, tyres and fuel yourself: quick checks that it's working today. Once a year a qualified mechanic does the MOT with special equipment. Decontamination is the same. You do the daily and weekly tests (automatic control, steam penetration, air leakage, protein residue) and write them down. The Competent Person (Decontamination) or engineer does the quarterly thermometric tests and the annual revalidation. And like an MOT certificate, the logbook proves it was done.

blocks.text: A colour change on a pouch is like the 'checked' sticker on a parcel: it shows it went through the system, not that what's inside is perfect.

explain.body: All benchtop sterilizers: automatic control test. Vacuum sterilizers (B and S) also: a steam penetration test (Helix or Bowie-Dick). Record temperature, pressure, date and signature.

test.q: Which pair of tests should be done daily on a type B sterilizer?
test.why: Type B sterilizers need a steam penetration test and an automatic control test every day.

whyNot.2: These are quarterly or annual tests by an engineer.
whyNot.3: These are tests for washers and ultrasonic cleaners.

explain.body: Weekly: air leakage (B, S), residual air (S, N), plus protein residue tests on washer-disinfectors and ultrasonics. Quarterly: thermometric tests and the ultrasonic activity test by a CP(D) or engineer. Annually: full revalidation.

items.label: Air leakage, residual air, protein residue

test.q: Which is a WEEKLY test on a vacuum sterilizer?
test.why: The air leakage test is done weekly by the user on type B and S sterilizers.

whyNot.1: Overheat cut-out is tested annually by an engineer.
whyNot.3: Thermometric tests are quarterly and annual.

explain.body: Checks an ultrasonic cleaner is active across the whole tank. Nine foil strips in a 3 × 3 grid, run for the set time. Similar erosion on all nine is a pass; markedly different or no erosion means withdraw it.

test.q: What result shows an ultrasonic cleaner has PASSED a foil ablation test?
options: Holes only in the centre strip
Similar erosion on all nine strips
Erosion on the outer eight strips only
test.why: Maximum erosion should be at similar positions and to a similar extent on all nine foils.

whyNot.1: Erosion in one place only shows uneven activity.
whyNot.3: Uneven erosion shows poor uniformity of cleaning.

explain.body: Each machine has a logbook: maintenance, validation, faults, modifications, routine tests. Record every cycle. Copy fading print-outs. Keep records at least two years. Audit decontamination at least every six months.

test.q: How long should sterilizer cycle records be kept, as a minimum, under HTM 01-05?
test.why: HTM 01-05 recommends that records be maintained for not less than two years.

whyNot.0: Three months is far too short.
whyNot.1: Six months is the audit interval, not record retention.
whyNot.2: One year is less than the recommended minimum.
